headline: Bay bakes past 78, and the doormats bail for the inlet
subhead: Great South Bay ran hot enough to push the fluke out to Fire Island Inlet and the ocean side — and a building new-moon tide should only sharpen that bite this week.
body_markdown:
Let me tell you what the bay looked like last week — flat, hazy, and warm enough to make you want to jump in with your clothes on. Great South Bay pushed up to 78.8 degrees in the shallows, which sounds great until you remember fluke don't love bathwater. That heat sat on the flats around Nicoll Bay and off Sayville for the better part of a week with light wind and not much to stir it, and by Thursday the guys who'd been picking at keepers on the West Fire Island flats were coming back with nothing but snappers and sea robins. The fish didn't disappear. They just did what smart fluke do — they slid for cooler water, and the cooler water right now is in the channels and out at the inlet.

That's set up the week ahead nicely, because we're building toward a new moon on the 13th, and that means spring tides stacking in through the weekend. Bigger swings at Fire Island Inlet, more water moving on the outgoing, and more of that upwelled ocean water — sitting around 71 degrees off the beach — getting pulled through Democrat Point and up into the channel edges off Robert Moses. When the bay's too warm and the ocean's noticeably cooler, that thermal seam right at the inlet mouth becomes the highway. Bait gets squeezed through it, and so do the fluke that are chasing it. I'd rather fish a strong outgoing at the inlet this week than putter around the bay flats hoping for a fluke that's already left the building.

And that's exactly how it's fished. The Robert Moses bridges — both the Route 27 span and the causeway pilings — have been holding fluke stacked on the outgoing, 25 to 35 feet depending where you set up on the drift. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails have been the honest producer, dragged slow right along bottom, with a few guys upsizing to chartreuse when the water's got any color to it after a tide change. Fish to five and a half pounds have come off that structure in the last week, mixed in with a lot of shorts, so it's not a pin-your-limit bite — it's a work-for-it bite, but the quality fish are legitimately there when you find the right piece of structure on the drift.

Democrat Point has been the better story for stripers, though I want to be straight with you — it's early mornings only right now, and it's not every morning. The bass are working the surf line off the point and down toward the lighthouse jetty on the last of the outgoing and into the start of the incoming, chasing bunker schools that have been pushing bait right up against the beach. Bucktails with white or pearl curly-tail trailers, and if you've got peanut bunker on hand, a fish-finder rig cast just outside the wash has been the better bet at first light. Bluefish have been mixed in with those schools too — nothing giant, mostly 2 to 4 pounds, but they'll test your leader and keep the rod bent while you're waiting on a bass to show. That bite has a short window. Once the sun's up and the wind picks up off the ocean, it shuts down fast.

Porgies have held steady in the bay — not exciting, but honest fishing if you want a bucket of fish for the pan. Bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig around the reef structure off Patchogue and the deeper holes toward Nicoll's Point have been producing steady action, better on the last two hours of the incoming when the current slows enough for the porgies to sit and feed instead of getting pushed around.

Weakfish, I'll be honest with you — it's been quiet. The water's been warm enough for weeks now, well above what we usually think weakfish need, and I keep hearing guys say "any day now," but any day hasn't come. I'm not writing them off completely for late summer, but if you're planning a trip around weakfish specifically this week, I'd have a strong Plan B.

Worth keeping an eye on for those of you who run east: the ocean-side eastern inlets have started throwing the season's first bonito and Spanish mackerel reports, riding clean incoming water. That's not squarely our patch out of Captree, but if you're trailering toward Moriches or beyond on a clean day, don't be shocked if something fast and silver hits your spoon.

Looking at the week ahead, I'm watching that new moon build through the weekend and thinking about the outgoing at Fire Island Inlet — bigger tide swings should push more of that 71-degree ocean water through and keep pulling fluke off the bay flats and onto the channel edges where we can actually catch them. If I had one morning to fish, I'd be at Robert Moses on the start of the outgoing with bucktails rigged and ready, and I'd have the surf rod in the truck just in case those bunker schools are still working the beach at first light. Two different bites, same tide window — that's about as good as July gets out here.
